etymologies.etymologyHTML: Ultimately from Latin repressus, the perfect passive participle of reprimō (“I repress”).

definitions.definition: (transitive) To forcefully prevent an upheaval from developing further.
(transitive, by extension) To check; to keep back.

quote.citation: 1671, John Milton, “The Second Book”, in Paradise Regain’d. A Poem. In IV Books. To which is Added, Samson Agonistes, London:  […]  J[ohn] M[acock] for John Starkey […], →OCLC, page 37, lines 542–544:
quote.text: Deſire of wine and all delicious drinks  […]  Thou couldſt repreſs,

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From re- +‎ press.

quote.citation: 2019, Niall Williams, This is Happiness, Bloomsbury (2020), pages 300-301:
quote.text: It had been a fraught car journey. From it my abiding memory is Charlie Troy having a deep but short-lived relationship with a smoking cigarette, rummaging after in the depthless depth of a shiny black handbag for a forbidden lipstick, finding it, applying it in Heaney’s mirror with a magician’s dexterity that defied the inconsistencies of the road, pressing, unpressing, and repressing her lips until the look came to her satisfaction and the bow was drawn.

definitions.definition: A record pressed again; a repressing.

quote.citation: 2010, Clinton Heylin, Bootleg! The Rise And Fall Of The Secret Recording Industry:
quote.text: Save for the shows he actually taped — Dylan, Springsteen, Page & Plant and other kindred spirits — his own titles by 1994 were just represses of hard-to-find Japanese or American titles.
